places.name: Tuyền Phòng
places.look: A low rise on the open grassland by the shore of Triêu Hà Hồ carries a short stack of pale timber halls and a three-roofed pagoda. Below the pagoda a round basin of white stone brims with spring water under one enormous wutong (ngô đồng) tree, its broad leaves always beaded wet. Stoneware jars sealed with red clay stand in rows on the lowest terrace, warming in the sun.
places.lore: Tuyền Phòng, the Spring House, is the old seat of Lễ Tuyền Phái, the healers' sect under Phượng Minh Cung, and the brewers keep it now: the sweet spring the phoenix is said to drink from, the cellars and the wine-masters' families are here. Nhạc Thuần Nhưỡng is its wine-master, and the brewers fill the hundred jars of spirit wine (linh tửu) the Pivot orders each year. Disciples may not draw from the basin with metal; they use gourds, so that the spring is never cut. The healers went down to the Dawn Hall on Triêu Hà Hồ in 1141.
places.history: In 660, in the Age of the North Star Compact, healers who brewed wine from the sweet spring founded Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the lake, under the protection of Phượng Minh Cung. Two years later, in 662, the green meadows of Lục Dã were given to the school for its herb gardens. For two centuries it stayed small, known in the rice towns for fevers cured and wounds washed clean. In 850 Mai Lễ Tuyền was born in Lục Dã Trấn, and it was said her first cry made the spring flow sweeter; she grew up to lead the school. Through the Age of Vein Wars its healers tended the wounded of their lord's short wars and took no side of their own. In 1140 its spirit wine was served at the Pivot's table for the first time, and Thiên Xu Tông set a standing yearly order for it. Envoys of the Pivot now come to the spring each year to fetch the jars.
places.art_brief: A small vertical miniature on flat golden grassland at a lake edge: a three-roofed pagoda over two stepped terraces of pale timber halls with dark grey-green tile roofs, the tallest outline on its plain. At its foot a round white stone spring basin under one huge spreading wutong tree with broad leaves; rows of brown stoneware jars with red clay seals along the lowest terrace; a thin stone channel running from the basin to the lake shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, soft shadows to the lower right, glints on the water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second pagoda roof and a wine cellar dug into the rise; the spring basin gains a carved stone canopy and a covered walk runs down to the lake.
The whole rise is terraced with herb courts and a guest hall for the Pivot's envoys; a white balustrade rings the wutong and a long jar store lines the shore.

places.name: Lai Nghi Thành
places.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the dry eastern steppe, its harbour mole curving out into the gulf. On the mole rises a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers, each crowned with a bronze bell frame, so that the whole stair glints at sunrise. A faint shimmer over the walls marks the city's guardian array (hộ thành trận).
places.lore: Phượng Minh Cung founded the city in 530 on the plain where, the old book says, the phoenix comes when the music is played nine times. Every dawn the city's musicians climb the nine tiers and play the same welcome nine times over, one tier at a time, whether or not anything comes. Harbour folk say the phoenix came once, long ago, and argue about which dawn it was. Ships of the gulf put in for rice from the plain and leave with lacquer and bronze.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Lai Nghi Thành in 530, soon after it took the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên, empty since the fall of Cửu Thiều. The name came from the old line about the Shao music played nine times, and the founders raised the bell terrace before the walls were finished. In the decades that followed the city became the Palace's door on the sea, and the guardian array was set over its walls. Once Hoàng Vân Thành was built upriver the grain barges came down to its quays, and in the great seven-year drought its harbour shipped the plain's rice to the hungry south. When Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the city manned its walls every night until the Pirate Purge swept the gulf clean. It has grown quietly rich on the coastal trade ever since. Old musicians say Cửu Thiều's music was never truly lost, only scattered to the four coasts, and that some of it came home here.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a flat dry steppe shore at a river mouth: rectangular walls of pale stone, grey-tile roofs with a few red-lacquered halls, a curved harbour mole reaching into blue water. The signature, and the tallest element, is a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers on the mole, each tier topped by a small bronze bell frame catching the light. A barely visible golden shimmer over the walls for the array. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows to the lower right. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The nine-tier terrace gains a roofed musicians' gallery and the harbour a second mole lined with warehouses.
A second wall ring takes in the river quays; the terrace is faced in red-lacquered stone and a tall ceremonial gate opens on the sea.

places.name: Hoàng Vân Thành
places.look: A broad walled city on the river where the rice plain lies flattest, crowned inside its walls by a ring of tall round granaries capped in yellow-glazed tile. At harvest a haze of rice chaff hangs over the roofs and turns gold in the low sun, which gives the city its name. Grain barges crowd the river quay below the granary gates.
places.lore: This is Phượng Minh Cung's granary city, and its keepers count grain the way other cities count gold. When the seven-year drought struck in 649 its granaries fed the whole south, and the Palace's power has rested on its rice ever since. In 1060 it opened its doors to Băng Tâm's desert in a famine year, and the old quarrel of the Desert Road was quietly let go. Every granary keeper swears an oath at the river never to sell the last basket.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung founded Hoàng Vân Thành in 600 as the granary of the rice plain of Triêu Dương Nguyên. Its first round granaries were raised along the river, where the barges of Thủy Điền and the inland villages could reach them. In 649 a drought began that lasted seven years; the granaries were opened and fed the south until the rains came back. That drought made the Palace's rice its strength, and granary after granary was added in the years that followed. In the Desert Road War, Phượng Minh and Băng Tâm Các fought over the caravan road between the desert and this plain, and the city's grain carts rolled to the front instead of the markets. The truce the Pivot imposed brought the caravans back, but the bitterness lasted for centuries. In 1060, in a famine year in the desert, the granaries were opened to Băng Tâm's people, and the quarrel was quietly forgotten. Its keepers still tell that story to every new apprentice.
places.art_brief: A broad, low walled city miniature on flat green-gold rice plain beside a river: rectangular grey walls, grey-tile roofs, and inside them a ring of tall round brick granaries with conical yellow-glazed tile caps, the signature and tallest element. A pale golden haze of chaff hanging low over the roofs; a river quay with a few grain barges at the base. Warm golden-hour light from the top left makes the yellow caps glow. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second ring of granaries rises outside the walls and a stone grain wharf runs along the river.
A walled granary district with a yellow-roofed counting hall at its heart; a canal basin is cut from the river for the barges.

places.name: Đạo Hương Trấn
places.look: A small walled town of grey-tile roofs in a sea of rice, the smell of ripening grain heavy on the river wind. Along the field road outside the east gate stands a long row of carved stone stakes, one for each generation of the Vương family, each beside the paddy that generation planted.
places.lore: The Vương family, rivals of the Tạ in another land, settled here in 520, and every generation since has planted one new field and set its stone, carved with the planter's name and the year's first rain. In the last days of 1199 the Vương sent a letter of betrothal to the Tạ of Phong Lâm. The town is still waiting for the reply, and its matchmakers are keeping very quiet.
places.art_brief: A small low town miniature inside rectangular earthen walls: a cluster of grey-tile roofs among flooded green rice paddies by a river. The signature is a long straight row of small carved standing stones along the field road outside one gate, each beside its own paddy. Water mirrors in the paddies; warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The Vương build an ancestral hall facing the row of stones, and the town walls are faced in brick.
A second walled quarter for rice merchants and a stone-paved field road; the row of generation stones now runs to the river.

places.name: Lục Dã Trấn
places.look: A walled town in open green meadows, ringed by a chequer of square herb beds in a dozen shades of green, each bordered by a low stone channel of spring water. In the morning the beds steam faintly and smell of mint and bitter root.
places.lore: Since 662 the meadows of Lục Dã have belonged to Lễ Tuyền Phái, which grows its healing herbs here. Mai Lễ Tuyền, the school's head, was born in the town in 850, and the townsfolk say her first cry made the spring flow sweeter. Mothers still bring newborns to the spring channel at the town gate for a first wash, hoping for the same luck.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on bright green meadow: rectangular walls, grey-tile roofs, and around them the signature chequerboard of square herb beds in many greens, edged by thin glinting stone water channels. A small gate with a spring channel running out of it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left; soft morning steam over the beds. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A drying pavilion for herbs and a walled seed garden of Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the town.
A brick-walled town with a healers' hall at the gate, and the herb chequer spread far across the meadows.

places.name: Thủy Điền Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-tile houses on a low dyke between flooded paddies, beside the river. On the bank a great bamboo waterwheel, its rim strung with tube buckets, creaks round and lifts water into the oldest fields on the plain.
places.lore: Rice was first planted on this plain in 140, in the flooded fields of Thủy Điền, and its paddies are older than every sect but two. Farmers here measure age in harvests, not years. Each spring, before any other village plants, a child of Thủy Điền sets the first seedling, and the plain follows.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs strung along a raised earth dyke between mirror-bright flooded paddies at a river bank. The signature is a tall bamboo waterwheel on the bank, its rim of tube buckets catching the light, spilling water into a channel. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone sluice; a barn for seed rice stands on the dyke.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the first rice and a row of wheels along the bank.

places.name: Âu Lộ Thôn
places.look: A low marsh shore of the eastern gulf, where a stand of dead trees is white with nesting gulls and herons and loud from dawn to dusk. The village houses sit back from the waterline on the landward edge of the marsh, and on their walls hang old diving baskets and weighted ropes, dry for centuries.
places.lore: Fishers say the birds were here before the sects and will be after. In 763, after Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng, the harbour's pearl divers settled here on the inland side of the marsh, away from the open sea, and never dived again. Their descendants fish only from the shore and hang an empty diving basket above every new door.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat salt-marsh shore: a few grey-tile roofs set back on the landward edge, reeds and mudflats between them and the sea. The signature is a stand of bare dead trees nearest the water, crowned white with nesting birds. Small dry wicker baskets hang on the house walls. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a shimmer on the tidal channels. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A boardwalk across the marsh to a small fishing jetty; the divers' quarter gains a shrine to the pearl harbour.
A walled fishing hamlet with drying racks along the shore; the heron trees are fenced and left untouched.

places.name: Ngân Hạnh Thôn
places.look: A forest village on a small river among the oak woods at the plain's edge, its grey roofs gathered under one colossal ginkgo (ngân hạnh) that dwarfs them. In autumn the tree turns gold in a single night, and by morning the roofs are carpeted yellow.
places.lore: The ginkgo is older than the village, which grew up around it. Every autumn the villagers sit up to see the night it turns, and no one has yet managed it. Its roasted nuts are sold on the road, and children are warned that greedy eaters get bad dreams.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature in temperate woodland by a small river: a few grey-tile roofs clustered beneath one enormous ginkgo tree, the signature, its fan-leaf crown bright gold and taller than everything around. Yellow leaves scattered on the roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left makes the crown blaze. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A roofed bench ring around the ginkgo's trunk and a stone bridge over the river.
A walled hamlet with a small temple at the ginkgo's foot and an inn for the road.

places.name: Lý Hoa Thôn
places.look: A fishing hamlet on a sandy beach, its boats drawn up below an orchard of white plum (lý hoa) that runs right down to the high-tide line. In early spring the orchard is so white that beach and blossom are hard to tell apart, and grey snow geese sit among the branches.
places.lore: Plum blossom here is so white that snow geese land among it by mistake, a tale told since 560. The villagers leave the geese alone, and say a goose that wakes in a plum tree brings a good catch.
places.art_brief: A tiny coastal village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs and small boats on a pale sandy beach, behind them the signature, an orchard of white-blossoming plum trees running down to the waterline, with a few grey geese among the blossom. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, soft blue sea at the base. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A stone landing for the boats and a pickling shed for plums.
A small walled harbour hamlet; the orchard is terraced up the dunes behind it.

places.name: Hoàng Ngưu Thôn
places.look: A cattle village on the open plain, its grey roofs gathered beside a great round corral of piled fieldstone. Yellow oxen graze in loose herds all around, and the grass near the corral is worn to bare earth.
places.lore: Yellow oxen ran wild on the plain left empty after Cửu Thiều fell, and in 400 the village that tamed them took their name. Its oxen pull ploughs and barges across much of the rice plain. On the first day of spring the herders paint one ox's horns red and walk it round the corral to bless the year.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on open grassland: a few grey-tile roofs beside the signature, a large circular corral wall of piled grey fieldstone with a worn earth floor, a few yellow-brown oxen as specks inside and around it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long grass shadows. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second corral and a roofed ox market beside the road.
A walled hamlet with a tannery and a shrine to the ox at the corral gate.

places.name: Lễ Tuyền Phái
places.look: A wide shallow lake lies so still at dawn in the open grassland that the first clouds lie doubled on it, a rose mist lifting off the water. On its shore stands the Dawn Hall, pale timber halls at the water's edge with herb terraces behind, and in the eastern shallows lies a low flat platform of weathered stone, half awash.
places.lore: Lễ Tuyền Phái, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of healers under Phượng Minh Cung, keeps its Dawn Hall (Triêu Đường) on this shore, where in 950 Mai Lễ Tuyền delivered Hoa Triêu Dương, now head of Phượng Minh Cung, at dawn as the clouds turned red. Mai Lễ Tuyền raised the hall in 1141 with a gift from the palace head and moved the healers and the inner gate down from the spring, while the brewers kept the Spring House. A bronze mirror that came with the gift hangs under the hall's eaves and gathers the lake's dawn light. The plain folk say the east's dawn clouds answer Lạc Hà's sunset clouds in the west, and pilgrims of the Palace come at dawn to watch them.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates the musicians of Vân Môn Thành, Cửu Thiều Cung's city on the plain, came to this lake to play to the rising sun. By 200 it was said that the dawn clouds took the colour of their music, and the players built a low stone platform in the shallows to stand on. After the War of the Nine Shao the musicians were gone, and for nearly two centuries only herders saw the dawns here. When Phượng Minh Cung took the plain, its people came back to the shore. In the Age of the North Star Compact healers founded Lễ Tuyền Phái beside the lake, at the sweet spring. In 950 Hoa Triêu Dương was born at dawn on the shore as the clouds turned red; a century and a half later she became head of Phượng Minh Cung. Since then pilgrims of the Palace come at dawn to watch the clouds, and some bring flutes.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a broad, calm, shallow lake in flat grassland, its surface mirroring rose and gold clouds, a soft pink mist lifting off the water. The signature is a low, flat, square platform of weathered grey stone, half awash in the eastern shallows, with rose light reflected on its wet surface. Reeds at the margins. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Vân Môn Thành
places.look: Low grass-grown walls on the river, broken into a rough square, with the stumps of towers at the corners. In the middle stands the one thing still upright: a tall frame of two carved stone pillars and a crossbeam, where the stone chime Vân Môn Khánh hung in the city's hall.
places.lore: Cửu Thiều Cung built Vân Môn Thành in 130 and named it for the Vân Môn music, twin of the Thiều. When Cửu Thiều fell the city emptied within a year, and its people took the music with them to the four coasts. Herders who shelter in the ruin say the empty frame hums a low note in a strong wind, and they will not sleep under it.
places.history: In 130 Cửu Thiều Cung, the palace of court music on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh, built Vân Môn Thành on the rice plain it had taken under its protection ten years before. The stone chime Vân Môn Khánh was hung in the city's hall, and the city became the plain's centre of music and trade. Its musicians played to the dawn at Triêu Hà Hồ, and the rice of Thủy Điền filled its markets. At the end of the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu Tông destroyed Cửu Thiều Cung in the War of the Nine Shao. In 341 Vân Môn Thành emptied within a year; its people scattered to the four coasts and took the music with them. Through the Age of Seven Seats its walls fell slowly while wild oxen grazed its streets. Phượng Minh Cung took the plain two centuries later but never resettled the city, and it lies in the Palace's land as a ruin. Whether the chime still lies under the rubble, no one on the plain will say for sure.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on flat grassland by a river: a rough square of low, grass-grown, crumbling walls with broken tower stumps at the corners and tumbled stones inside. The signature and tallest element is a tall freestanding frame of two carved grey stone pillars with a crossbeam, standing alone in a roofless hall. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left casting a long shadow of the frame. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Châu Lệ Cảng
places.look: A curve of low coast where a beach of heaped white oyster shells glitters under rows of charred pier pilings standing in the shallows. Behind them the burned shells of warehouses and a broken harbour wall slope down into the sea.
places.lore: Phượng Minh Cung built the pearl harbour here in 600, and for over a century its divers brought up the pearls of the moonlit sea. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned it; the divers fled, and the pearls in the sea are said to weep. Fishers passing on moonlit nights say the water over the old oyster beds glows faintly, and they do not stop.
places.history: Phượng Minh Cung built Châu Lệ Cảng on its eastern coast in 600, the same year it founded Hoàng Vân Thành, to bring in the pearls of the gulf. Its divers worked the oyster beds off the shell beach, and its pearls went to the Palace's hall and the markets of the coast. A generation later Ô Kình Hải founded Thôn Hải Môn on an islet of the southern gulf, and the pearl harbour lay within reach of his ships. In 762 Thôn Hải's pirates burned Châu Lệ Cảng. The divers fled, and the next year they settled inland at Âu Lộ and never dived again. The pirates were destroyed in the Pirate Purge two decades later, but no one came back to rebuild. The shell beach is all that is left, and the saying that the pearls weep has outlived the harbour.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature on a low grassy coast: a curved beach of heaped white oyster shells, rows of blackened broken pier pilings standing up out of shallow turquoise water, the roofless fire-scarred walls of a few warehouses and a broken harbour wall sloping into the sea. The tallest elements are the charred pilings and a broken wall corner. Warm golden-hour light from the top left glinting on the shells. No roofs, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Vũ Lâu
places.look: Out of the rain forest rises a dormant volcanic cone, dark with banana groves on its terraced flanks, and on its crown a slender many-eaved tower, the tallest thing in the south. From every eave of every storey hang long bronze rain-chains, so that in a downpour the whole tower runs with water and rings like a struck bell. No lamp burns in any window.
places.lore: Vũ Lâu, the Rain Tower, is the old seat of Thính Vũ Lâu, a great sect (đại tông môn) of the ma đạo (demonic path) that carried its halls east to Thần Cổ Phong in 1166-1170. The first elder Quan Vũ Thanh stays in the founder's tower with the founder's chain on the eaves, and from it the Tower governs the south: the cities, four of the five vassals and the Night Rain Market's tax. The lake graves of Tàn Hà Hồ lie below, and a copy of the founder's sutra is kept here. Phó Tiêu Tương built the tower so that one could listen to the rain, and since the masters of the ma đạo came by night after the Night Rain Edict its lamps have never been lit.
places.history: Phó Tiêu Tương founded Thính Vũ Lâu in the rain forests in 380. A century later, when Khải Lôi Môn fell, the Tower rose on its ground and took the thunder mountains. It won the forest half of the Petal Shore by the Pivot's judgement, then broke the Compact beside Lạc Hà in the War of Broken Halberds and lost. In 880 Phó Tiêu Tương died, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ took the headship and the Tương Phi Tán; in 905 he proclaimed the Night Rain Edict. In 906 the ma đạo masters came by night, Cố Dạ Lan among them, and the lamps were never lit again. Beaten at Đan Sơn Mạch, the Tower had rebuilt its strength twice over by 1165, to the Pivot's unease. In 1185 its first elder Quan Vũ Thanh went in secret to Phượng Minh to talk of peace, and came back without an answer.
places.art_brief: The tallest outline in its land: a dark dormant volcanic cone with terraced banana groves on its flanks, crowned by a slender many-storeyed tower of dark timber and black-grey tile, every eave hung with long bronze rain-chains that catch the light; stepped halls on narrow terraces climbing one side of the cone; all windows dark. A thin veil of rain cloud trailing from the summit. Warm golden-hour light from the top left gleams on wet leaves and bronze. No lit lamps or lanterns, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: New halls stack up the cone's flank on black stone terraces, each roof hung with its own rain-chains, and a covered stair climbs from the lake.
A second, lower tower rises on a shoulder of the cone, joined to the first by a roofed bridge; the whole slope is walled in dark stone, and still no window shows a light.

places.name: Nhã Môn
places.look: Where the rain forest meets the sea, a walled manor of red-lacquered halls rises in three terraces, half buried in glossy leaves. Its entrance is a perfect round moon gate of red lacquer, so thickly wreathed in vines of scarlet, black-eyed beans that the lacquer barely shows. A path of crushed shell leads to it from the forest road.
places.lore: Nhã Môn, the Gracious Door, is the front house of Hồng Đậu Trang on the forest road, a minor ma đạo sect under Thính Vũ Lâu, and it keeps the tea room that opens to guests of every sect. Liễu Đa Thải, mistress of the door, pours each guest one cup and decides who is poured a second. Nghê Hồng Đậu moved her own rooms and her canon to the vein garden in 1110, and only a cart track from here reaches it. The house is famous for its hospitality, and it is said that those who stay too long do not leave.
places.history: In the early years of the North Star Compact, Diệp Phi Hồng, sworn sister of Lạc Anh Phái's new head, kept the sword Phi Hồng when the school's founder died without naming an heir. More than a century later, long after Lạc Anh had broken apart, she carried Phi Hồng into the rain forest of Tiêu Vũ Lâm and taught its art to no one, and the sword waited there for an heir. In 800 Nghê Hồng Đậu was born in Thu Trì Thành, and red beans grew from the cracks in her mother's doorstep. In 910 she found Phi Hồng where Diệp Phi Hồng had left it, and founded Hồng Đậu Trang around it under the lordship of Thính Vũ Lâu. By 912 the manor's gracious door was open to guests from every sect, and the saying began that those who stay too long do not leave. Its poisons and charms found ready buyers once the Night Rain Market opened in Thu Trì the next century. In 1197 travellers on the forest road found red beans scattered on the path to the manor, and stepped around them; no one has said what they meant.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat miniature at the edge of dark green jungle above a small shore: three terraces of red-lacquered halls with dark tile roofs climbing a gentle slope, a short red pagoda at the top as the tallest element. The signature is a round red moon gate at the bottom terrace, almost hidden under vines hung with scarlet beans; a pale crushed-shell path leading to it. Glossy broad leaves crowding the walls. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A guest wing on stilts over the shore and a walled poison garden behind the halls; the moon gate gains a twin on the sea side.
Three walled courts climb the slope to a red pagoda where Phi Hồng is kept; the bean vines now cover the whole outer wall.

places.name: Thu Trì Thành
places.look: A walled port city where a river meets the sea below wooded hills, built in steps so that tiers of square stone pools descend through its streets from the upper town to the harbour. After night rain on the hills every pool brims and spills into the next, and the whole city murmurs. Over the lower terraces hang the dark oiled-paper awnings of the Night Rain Market, and a guardian array (hộ thành trận) shimmers faintly on the walls.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 400 and named it for the old poem of night rain on the mountain swelling the autumn pools. Since 1000 it has held the Night Rain Market, which sells ma đạo pills, poisons and arts that no other city allows; it opens only after dark and only in rain, and buyers come from as far as the desert. Innkeepers here learned long ago not to ask names. Nghê Hồng Đậu and the head's disciple Mạnh Lưu Ly were both born within its walls.
places.history: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Thu Trì Thành in 400, twenty years after its own founding, as its port on the southern sea. The stone pools were cut into the slope to catch the night rain off the hills, and the forest's honey, timber and grain went out from its harbour. In 800 Nghê Hồng Đậu was born here, and red beans grew from the cracks in her mother's doorstep. After the Night Rain Edict, strangers in black came up the forest road at night for the whole of 908, and the innkeepers learned not to ask their names. In 1000 the Tower opened the Night Rain Market in the city, and its treasury doubled within fifty years. By 1005 the market was known to open only after dark and only in rain, and it drew buyers from as far as the desert. In 1060 Mạnh Lưu Ly was born here, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ took her as his disciple.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a gentle slope between wooded hills and the sea at a river mouth: grey-tile roofs in stepped rows, and the signature, a descending stair of square stone pools brimming with water between the streets, spilling from tier to tier down to the harbour. Dark oiled-paper awnings over the lowest terraces; a faint shimmer of array light along the walls; a few boats at the quay. Wet surfaces after rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking through. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The pools climb higher up the hill as the upper town grows; a second harbour basin and a long covered hall for the Night Rain trade.
A walled upper city of dark halls looks down over the tiered pools; the market's awnings spread across three terraces and the harbour is walled in stone.

places.name: Bình Dã Trấn
places.look: A walled town in an open plain cleared from the forest, its grey roofs gathered around a huge paved yard of sun-baked brick. On dry days the yard is covered edge to edge with mats of drying tea, herbs, cloth and grain brought in from the wet country around.
places.lore: Bình Dã became a town in 410 on the one open plain in the south where it rarely rains. Forest folk carry their wet harvests here to dry, and the town lives on the fees. When rain does come, the yard-keepers beat a gong and the whole town runs out to roll up the mats.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on a dry open grassland clearing with rain forest at its edges and a river nearby: rectangular walls and grey-tile roofs around the signature, a large square paved brick yard covered in a patchwork of drying mats in green, brown and ochre. A small gong frame at the yard's edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a clear sky over the town and darker cloud at the forest margins. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second drying yard outside the walls and roofed sheds to store the mats.
A brick-walled town with a raised drying terrace on every rooftop and a merchants' hall facing the great yard.

places.name: Xuân Thảo Thành
places.look: A city on a river at the forest's edge, enclosed by thick earthen walls whose tops are capped with living turf, green even in the dry months. Inside, grey-tile roofs stand among young trees, and in the meadows outside the walls old blackened stumps lie grown over with grass.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded Xuân Thảo Thành in 640 on the forest land the Pivot gave it after the Petal Shore fighting. Its people take their name from the old line that wildfire cannot burn out the grass, for the spring wind brings it back. Every spring the citizens recut and replant the turf on the walls together, and it is a festival day. The charred stumps in the meadows are left untouched.
places.history: The land of Xuân Thảo was once forest on the edge of Lạc Anh Phái's Petal Shore. When Lạc Anh split, Lạc Hà Tông and Thính Vũ Lâu both claimed the empty shore, and their disciples fought in the burning orchards. Fire swept the land, and Hồng Vũ Thành burned, its petals and ashes falling together like red rain. Then the Pivot's judgement gave the bay to Lạc Hà and the forest to Thính Vũ. Twenty years after the judgement, in 640, Thính Vũ founded Xuân Thảo Thành on ground the fighting had burned, where new grass had come up through the ash. The city grew as a market for the forest villages and a stop on the road from the Tower toward the coast. Its turf walls were never stormed, and through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed one of the Tower's quietest cities.
places.art_brief: A walled city miniature on green grassland by a river at a forest edge: thick earthen walls with rounded tops capped in bright living turf, the signature; inside, grey-tile roofs among young green trees and a modest gate tower as the tallest element. In the meadow outside, a few blackened tree stumps half hidden in grass. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second turf-capped wall ring and a stone bridge over the river with a market at its foot.
A walled forest-trade city with a timber hall on a grassy mound at its heart, its own roof turfed like the walls.

places.name: Kiều Bạn Thôn
places.look: Where the forest road crosses a slow river, a roofed timber bridge with deep eaves carries the traffic, and under those eaves hang rows of worn straw sandals. A cluster of grey-tile houses and an inn crowd its northern end.
places.lore: The village grew up around the crossing in 680 and took its name from the bridge. Travellers leave their worn-out sandals hanging under the eaves and buy new ones at the far end, so that their tiredness stays on the bridge. Once a year the village burns the old sandals on the bank.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature at a river crossing on grassland: a roofed wooden bridge with dark grey tile and deep eaves, the signature, rows of small straw sandals hanging under its eaves; a few grey-tile houses and an inn at one end. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, reflections in the slow water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second inn and a stone pier strengthening the bridge's middle.
A walled hamlet at the bridgehead with a sandal-makers' row and a small shrine to travellers.

places.name: Bình Độ Thôn
places.look: A ferry landing on a wide, slow forest river, where a broad flat raft with a small thatched sleeping shelter on its deck is poled across from a village of grey-tile houses. The water here is glassy and barely moves.
places.lore: The ferry at Bình Độ has been famous since 460 for being so calm that sleeping passengers are carried over without waking. Ferrymen never raise their voices on the river, and the village forbids drums on the bank. Travellers who are carried over asleep are woken on the far side with a cup of tea.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a grassy bank of a wide, mirror-calm river: a few grey-tile roofs at a wooden landing, and the signature, a broad flat ferry raft mid-river with a little thatched shelter on its deck. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, perfect reflections. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second raft and a stone landing stair; a tea house on the bank.
A walled hamlet at the landing with a covered waiting hall, and ferry landings on both banks.

places.name: Hoa Điền Thôn
places.look: A river village set among sweeping fields of flowers in long strips of purple, yellow and white. Along the village edge runs a wall of stacked hollow-log beehives, humming loudly all summer.
places.lore: Since 540 the flower fields of Hoa Điền have fed the bees of the rain forest, and its honey is sold in Thu Trì Thành. Beekeepers tell their bees every piece of village news, births and deaths first, or the bees will leave.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs by a river among long stripes of purple, yellow and white flower fields, and the signature, a low wall of stacked round hollow-log beehives along the village edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second hive wall and a honey-boiling shed by the river.
A walled hamlet with a wax-chandlers' row and a jetty for the honey boats to Thu Trì.

places.name: Yên Kiều Thôn
places.look: A river village in low meadows, where a long, narrow bridge of grey stone slabs on many low piers runs out across a misty river and fades into fog before it reaches the other side. On rainy days its far end cannot be seen at all.
places.lore: The misty bridge at Yên Kiều vanishes in the rain, and since 760 travellers who cross it have said it is longer than it looks. The village now belongs to Hồng Đậu Trang, whose guests pass this way. Locals cross only in pairs, holding a rope between them, and count their steps aloud.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature in low green meadow: a few grey-tile roofs on one bank, and the signature, a long low bridge of flat grey stone slabs on many small piers running out across the river and dissolving into a band of white mist. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the near bank, cool mist beyond. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A rope rail along the bridge and a small shrine at its near end.
A walled hamlet with an inn for Hồng Đậu Trang's guests; lamps of red glass on posts along the bridge.

places.name: Tàn Hà Hồ
places.look: A grey lake at the foot of the Tower's cone, its surface crowded with withered lotus: tall brown stalks, curled dry leaves and empty seedpods that are never cut and never cleared. Even in summer the lake looks like the end of autumn.
places.lore: Phó Tiêu Tương kept the withered lotus on the lake below her tower to listen to the rain on it, and the lake took the name Tàn Hà Hồ. Disciples of Thính Vũ sit on its shore in storms, learning to hear each drop on the dry leaves apart. No one may cut a stalk, and any lotus that blooms is left to wither.
places.history: Phó Tiêu Tương founded Thính Vũ Lâu above this lake, and in 382, two years after the founding, she kept the withered lotus standing on the lake below her tower so that she could listen to the rain on it, and the lake was named Tàn Hà Hồ. From then on the Tower's sword disciples were sent to its shore to listen to the rain before they were taught the sword. When the founder died five centuries later the lotus was left as she had kept it. After the Night Rain Edict the lake shore became the place where new masters were first received, by night. In 1158, after the Tower's defeat at Đan Sơn Mạch, Mạnh Dạ Vũ did not leave the Tower for a year, and in all that year the rain on Tàn Hà Hồ never stopped. Disciples still call a long rain a head's mourning.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a small grey-green lake in rain forest at the foot of a volcanic slope, its whole surface crowded with brown withered lotus, the signature, dry upright stalks, curled leaves and empty seedpods. Rain dimpling the water. Banana and forest leaves at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking under rain cloud. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hắc Hùng Lĩnh
places.look: A forested highland ridge above the rain forest, its slopes broken by boulders. At the mouth of a dark cave stands a tilted slab of grey rock scored with deep parallel claw marks, the black bears' scratching stone.
places.lore: Black bears den in the caves of this ridge and come down to the forest's honey trees in autumn. Woodcutters of Tiêu Vũ Lâm measure their courage by how close they will walk to the scratching stone. Hunters say the freshest claw marks show how big the den's master has grown.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a forested highland ridge with grey boulders and a dark cave mouth, before it the signature, a tilted grey rock slab gouged with deep parallel claw marks. Dense green canopy below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, deep shadow in the cave. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Xuyên Lâm Môn
places.look: On a high shoulder of Kinh Trập Sơn above the rain forest, a sect gate of plain grey stone stands at the head of a long stair that drops straight into the trees. Beside it an open-sided gatehouse holds racks of worn hardwood guide staffs, one taken down for every traveller led through the forest. Above the gate, small halls climb the ridge on narrow terraces.
places.lore: Xuyên Lâm Môn is a minor sect of staff fighters under Thính Vũ Lâu, who guide travellers through the rain forest and pay no heed to the rain beating the leaves. It is a chính đạo (righteous path) school under a ma đạo lord, and does not hide its dislike of the Tower's new arts. Its head, Úc Diệp Thanh, guided every traveller himself in his first year. A traveller returns the staff at the far end of the road, and the next guide carries it home.
places.history: Staff fighters who guided travellers through the rain forest founded Xuyên Lâm Môn in 690, in the Age of the North Star Compact, under the lordship of Thính Vũ Lâu. They took their name from an old line about paying no heed to the rain that pierces the forest and beats the leaves. Their footwork was trained in the bamboo of Đả Diệp Lâm below the gate, and their guides kept the forest roads open in war and peace. In 907 the school refused the arts of the Night Rain Edict, and its head walked the forest road alone for a month in protest. The Tower let the protest pass, and the school kept its own ways and its coastal town of Vọng Hải. In 1170 Úc Diệp Thanh became head and guided every traveller himself for a year. In 1199 an earthquake raised a river isle at Hà Châu, and Xuyên Lâm claimed it against its own lord.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat miniature on a steep forested mountain shoulder: small grey-stone halls with dark grey tile roofs stacked up a ridge on narrow terraces, a short pagoda at the top as the tallest element. At the bottom, a plain grey stone gate at the head of a long straight stair descending into dense green canopy, and beside it the signature, an open-sided gatehouse lined with racks of upright wooden staffs. Rain mist in the trees below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second staff house at the foot of the stair, and a roofed rest hall halfway down for travellers.
A walled mountain gate with a training court cut into the ridge and a covered stair running the full way down into the forest.

places.name: Không Mông Thành
places.look: A walled port city in a low valley mouth by the sea, almost always seen through fine hazy rain. Every street is roofed by long covered arcades of grey tile on red-painted posts, so that one can cross the whole city without getting wet. Above the arcades rise the older halls of Khải Lôi's time, their roof ridges capped in green bronze.
places.lore: Khải Lôi Môn founded the city in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, and Thính Vũ Lâu has held it since the Gate fell. Many of its families descend from the people of Lôi Trạch Thành, who came here after their own city burned. They still keep a thunder-day in spring, beating drums under the arcades when the first thunder is heard. The hills hazy in the rain are lovely too, the poem says, and painters come for it.
places.history: Khải Lôi Môn, the Gate That Opens the Thunder, founded Không Mông Thành in 200 in the hazy rain of its southern valleys, the same year Lý Thiên Cổ first beat the thunder drum Xuân Lôi Cổ. The city grew as the Gate's southern port, while Lôi Trạch Thành held the river mouth below the mountains. Nearly three centuries later Hầu Xuân Lôi was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. A year afterwards the people of Lôi Trạch moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành, and the arcades were raised over the streets to shelter the newcomers' stalls. The Gate never recovered, and Thính Vũ Lâu rose on its ground and took the city with the mountains. Through the Age of Vein Wars it has stayed a quiet trading port. Old families still whisper that the Gate's thunder inheritance lies sealed somewhere in the mountains above.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature in a low green valley mouth at the sea, seen through a soft veil of fine rain: rectangular walls, and the signature, long grey-tile covered arcades on red posts lining every street in a grid; above them a few older halls with green-bronze roof ridges as the tallest elements. A small harbour at the base. Warm golden-hour light from the top left diffused by the haze. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: The arcades reach the harbour quays, and a drum tower rises at the main crossing.
A second wall ring up the valley sides; covered bridges link the arcades across the river, and the harbour gains a stone breakwater.

places.name: Hạnh Hoa Thị
places.look: A market town on the river below the southern road to Thính Vũ Lâu, built of deep, narrow lanes between tall grey-tile houses. From every eave hang woven baskets of apricot blossom (hạnh hoa), so after rain the lanes are roofed in pink and white. Apricot trees crowd the river bank behind the stalls.
places.lore: The market grew up in 700 below Thính Vũ's southern road, and after a night of spring rain its lanes sell flowers, as the old poem of the small tower promises. It is also known for the healer Giả Hồi Xuân, born here in 1020, who cures what the alchemists of three sects would not touch. On mornings after rain the sick wait in the flower lanes alongside the buyers.
places.art_brief: A market town miniature on dry steppe by a river: rectangular walls around a tight grid of narrow deep lanes between tall grey-tile houses, the signature being woven baskets of pink and white blossom hanging from the eaves along every lane. Pink apricot trees along the river bank. Wet roofs after rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A covered flower hall at the market gate and a stone quay on the river.
A second walled quarter of healers and herb sellers; the apricot grove is walled as a market garden.

places.name: Lãng Hoa Thành
places.look: A walled port city on a dry, wind-bitten steppe coast at the mouth of a river. Its sea wall is pierced with rows of carved stone blowholes, and when the waves strike, white spray bursts from them in plumes like flowers along the whole waterfront. Behind the wall, grey roofs climb a low rise toward a watch hall.
places.lore: Thính Vũ Lâu founded the city in 800 on the sea-spray coast, once the Pirate Purge had made it safe at last. Its people are mostly fishers and salt-boilers who came down to the shore when the pirates were gone. On storm days children run along the wall racing the spray, and the one soaked by the biggest plume is called lucky for the year.
places.history: For centuries this coast lay nearly empty, open to the raiders of the southern gulf. Once Thôn Hải Môn was founded on its islet its sails came often, and the watchtowers of Vọng Hải learned to see them a day before they landed. Then the Pivot called the Pirate Purge, and it ended with Ô Kình Hải dead on his islet. Two decades later, in 800, while the War of Broken Halberds held the Tower's strength in the north, Thính Vũ Lâu founded Lãng Hoa Thành on the sea-spray coast, safe at last from pirates. Its builders cut the blowholes into the sea wall to break the force of the storm waves. With the Tower's eyes on the war, the young city grew up largely on its own. Since the Age of Vein Wars began it has been a fishing and salt port, far from the quarrels over veins.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature on a dry ochre steppe coast at a river mouth: grey-tile roofs climbing a low rise to a modest watch hall, the tallest element. The signature is the sea wall along the waterfront, pierced with a row of carved stone blowholes throwing up white plumes of spray like flowers. Salt pans at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left catching the spray. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second harbour mole with its own blowholes, and stone salt pans along the shore.
A walled upper town around the watch hall, and a long spray wall running the whole bay.

places.name: Vọng Hải Trấn
places.look: A walled town in coastal bamboo at a river mouth, below a line of low sea cliffs. Along the cliff tops stand tall watchtowers with stone footings and bamboo upper storeys, each with a signal frame looking out over the gulf.
places.lore: Vọng Hải belongs to Xuyên Lâm Môn, whose people keep the watchtowers manned. In 780 the towers saw Thôn Hải's sails a day before they landed, and the warning is still told as the saving of the coast. The town keeps a watch on every tower though no pirate has come in centuries, and a watcher caught asleep must carry water to every house.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature among green coastal bamboo at a river mouth, grey-tile roofs below low rocky sea cliffs. The signature is a row of tall watchtowers on the cliff tops, stone bases with bamboo upper storeys and small signal frames. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, blue sea at the base. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A walled signal post joins the towers along the cliffs, and a fishing harbour is dug in the river mouth.
A brick-walled coastal town with a beacon hall and a covered stair from the harbour to the towers.

places.name: Phong Đăng Trấn
places.look: A walled harbour town in fertile river meadows by the sea, its fields heavy with grain. In its main gate hangs a huge wooden steelyard balance, its beam as long as a boat, where grain carts are weighed for the tax before they enter.
places.lore: The Lục family's harvests at Phong Đăng are so rich that since 600 Thính Vũ has collected its grain tax here first each year. The first cart weighed on the great steelyard is always the Lục family's, and the whole town turns out to watch the beam. The neighbouring villages grumble that the beam is honest only once a year.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on rich green river meadows by the sea: grey-tile roofs inside rectangular walls, golden grain fields around. The signature is a massive wooden steelyard beam with a stone counterweight, hanging from a roofed frame over the main gate. A small harbour with grain boats. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A walled granary yard for the tax grain and a stone quay for the boats.
A brick-walled town with the Lục family's manor on a rise and a second steelyard over the harbour gate.

places.name: Ương Ca Thôn
places.look: A hill village above a river, its grey-tile houses at the top of a stair of curving rice terraces. At the head of the terraces stands a round stone stage open to the sky, where the singers stand at planting.
places.lore: Farmers have sung as they plant the terraces here since 540, and the song is the oldest in the south. Since Thu Phần Các came, the villagers hear singing from the graves of Lôi Trạch every autumn, and they sing louder at planting to drown it. Nobody in Ương Ca sings the planting song in autumn.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a gentle hillside above a river: a few grey-tile roofs at the top of curving, water-filled rice terraces stepping down the slope. The signature is a round flat stone stage at the head of the terraces. Warm golden-hour light from the top left mirrored in the terrace water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: More terraces cut down to the river, and a roof of thatch over the singing stage.
A walled hill hamlet with a hall of the planting song beside the stage.

places.name: Song Khê Thôn
places.look: A village where two brooks, one clear and one tea-brown from the forest, run together in a Y below the houses. On the point of land where they meet stands a tiny roofed shrine with two bamboo dippers tied together by a red cord.
places.lore: Lovers who drink from both brooks are said never to part, a belief recorded since 1000. Couples come from as far as Thu Trì to drink with the joined dippers. The village matchmaker keeps the cord and swears she has never had to replace it.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on grassland: a few grey-tile roofs above a Y-shaped meeting of two small brooks, one clear blue and one tea-brown. The signature is a tiny roofed shrine on the point of land where they join, with two small dippers joined by a red cord. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A pair of small stone bridges over both brooks and a wedding inn beside the shrine.
A walled hamlet with a lovers' pavilion over the confluence.

places.name: Thượng Độ Thôn
places.look: A ferry village on the upper river, where a ferry boat is hauled across on a rope strung between two tall carved stone posts. The post on the near bank is charred black to its top.
places.lore: In the Thunder Vein War of 1045, Phượng Minh's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. They burned the landing and scorched the stone post, which the villagers have never cleaned. The villagers say it is the nearest the Palace has come to the Tower's heart, and Thính Vũ's disciples stop here to look at it.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a grassy upland river bank: a few grey-tile roofs at a ferry landing, and the signature, two tall carved stone posts on either bank with a rope strung between them and a small boat on it; the near post blackened by fire. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A stone landing on both banks and a guard hut beside the charred post.
A walled hamlet with a small fort at the ferry, the charred post kept inside its gate.

places.name: Hà Châu Thôn
places.look: A river village of grey roofs on the bank, facing a raw new isle of grey mud and gravel that has risen in the middle of the river. Two rival boundary flags flap on the isle, one at either end.
places.lore: In 1199 an earthquake raised a river isle at Hà Châu out of the water, and Thính Vũ and Xuyên Lâm both claim it. Villagers row out each morning to see whose flag has been moved. Nothing grows on the isle yet, but everyone is sure something valuable will.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat river bank: a few grey-tile roofs and small boats, facing the signature, a bare new island of grey mud and gravel in midstream with two small differently coloured flags on poles at its two ends. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A jetty out to the isle and the first willows planted on it.
A walled hamlet across both bank and isle, joined by a wooden bridge.

places.name: Kinh Điện Khoáng
places.look: A mine on a bare ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, where open-air forges stand on the rock beside the pit mouths, each with a tall iron rod raised above it to catch the lightning. The rock around them is streaked with burn marks.
places.lore: Lightning strikes the ore of Kinh Điện so often that since 220 Khải Lôi's smiths forged in the storm. Thính Vũ's smiths keep the old forges and still wait for storms to work. Miners wear wooden shoes and never carry iron tools in the rain.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a bare grey mountain ridge: a few dark pit mouths, low stone forge hearths in the open, and the signature, tall iron lightning rods standing above each forge. Scorch streaks on the rock, a storm cloud edge above. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Tử Kim Khoáng
places.look: A mine on a steep mountain slope, its tunnel mouths set in cliffs streaked purple and gold. Below them long fans of purple-tinted spoil spill down the hillside.
places.lore: Purple-gold ore, the colour of storm light, has been dug at Tử Kim since 300. The metal takes an edge well and is prized by Thính Vũ's sword smiths. Miners say a seam glows faintly before a storm, and they leave the tunnels when it does.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a steep high-mountain slope: timber-framed tunnel mouths in a cliff banded with purple and gold streaks, and the signature, long fans of violet-tinted spoil spilling down the slope below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Vũ Hoa Khoáng
places.look: The highest mine in the thunder mountains, a stony upland where the stream beds have been dammed into long wooden sluices. In them lie heaps of smooth pebbles of every colour, red, agate-banded, green and white, gleaming wet in the rain.
places.lore: Rain-flower pebbles, said to be flowers that fell as rain while a master preached, were found here in 500, and Thính Vũ keeps the mine. It is held to be the richest mine ground in the Tower's mountains. Pickers sort the pebbles in the rain, when the colours show truest.
places.art_brief: A small mine miniature on a high stony upland: no tunnels, but the signature, long wooden sluices and dammed stream beds filled with heaps of wet, multicoloured pebbles in red, green, white and banded agate. Low stone sorting sheds as the only structures. Light rain, warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Liệt Khuyết Phong
places.look: The highest summit of Kinh Trập Sơn, a sheer grey peak split from crown to shoulder by a deep vertical rift, as if cut by one stroke. The rock along the rift is fused black and glassy, and storm clouds gather on it more often than on any other summit.
places.lore: The peak takes its name from an old poet's line of lightning and thunder under which the ridges crumble. Khải Lôi's disciples once climbed it in storms to invite the lightning; Thính Vũ's disciples now drill on it in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both, and lay a bowl of rice on the trail for each one who does not come down.
places.history: In the Age of First Gates, Khải Lôi Môn taught that a cultivator must invite the lightning, and this peak became its proving ground. By 440 the Gate's disciples were climbing it in storms, and only a third of them came down. The fused black rock along the rift is said to mark where the strongest strikes have landed. After Khải Lôi fell, the peak lay unused, and the mountain folk said its storms were waiting. Thính Vũ Lâu, whose arts lean toward Thunder, took up the old practice in its own way. By 1166, as the Tower rebuilt its strength after Đan Sơn Mạch, its disciples were drilling on Liệt Khuyết Phong in thunderstorms. The villagers below count the lightning and the disciples both.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline, the tallest summit of its range: a sheer grey rock peak split by a deep vertical rift from its crown, the rift's edges fused black and glassy. Snow streaks on the high ledges, a dark storm cloud pressed against the summit with a faint thread of lightning. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the lit face. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Đả Diệp Lâm
places.look: A grove of tall green bamboo on low hills, so dense that rain on the leaves roars like surf. In its heart is a clearing filled with cut bamboo stumps of different heights, standing in rows like a field of posts.
places.lore: The forest gives its line to Xuyên Lâm Môn nearby: pay no heed to the rain piercing the forest and beating the leaves. The school's young disciples train their footwork on the stumps in downpours, learning to keep their footing as the rain hammers the grove. Woodcutters who come for poles must leave the clearing alone.
places.history: The bamboo of Đả Diệp Lâm was old long before any sect came to Kinh Trập Sơn, and in Khải Lôi's day it was a wild grove that the Gate's people crossed on their way to the sea. After the Gate fell the grove passed into Thính Vũ Lâu's land, and woodcutters from the villages took its poles for houses and ferries. When Xuyên Lâm Môn was founded nearby in the Age of the North Star Compact, its staff fighters took the forest's line for their own and began to train in it. The clearing of stumps was cut in the school's early years, and every generation of disciples has recut it. In the year after the Night Rain Edict, while their head walked the forest road in protest against the Night Rain Edict, the disciples are said to have trained here through the whole rain in silence. A guide of Xuyên Lâm is still not trusted to lead travellers until they have crossed the stumps in a storm without falling.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a dense grove of tall green bamboo on low rounded hills, rain streaking through the leaves. The signature is a clearing at its heart filled with rows of cut bamboo stumps of many different heights, like a field of posts. Warm golden-hour light from the top left slanting through the rain. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Kinh Lôi Mạch
places.look: High on a bare black ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn, seams of violet light run through the rock like veins under skin, brightening whenever thunder rolls. Nothing grows on the ridge, and the air above it smells of a struck flint.
places.lore: Kinh Lôi Mạch is a spirit vein (linh mạch) that carries Thunder from the storm peaks, the richest prize in the mountains and close to Thiên Xu's border. Lệ Tiêu Hồn, master of the Tower's soul vaults, has kept it since 1010. Phượng Minh Cung fought for it from 1040 to 1046 and lost; the south remembers.
places.history: The vein runs within reach of the storm peaks of Kinh Trập Sơn, and its qi has carried Thunder for as long as anyone has drawn on it. Khải Lôi Môn's cultivators knew the ridge in the Age of First Gates, and after the Gate fell it passed with the mountains to Thính Vũ Lâu. In 1010 Lệ Tiêu Hồn broke through in the Tower's soul vaults, and Mạnh Dạ Vũ made him keeper of Kinh Lôi Mạch. In 1040 Phượng Minh Cung went to war with Thính Vũ Lâu for the vein. In the war's last year the Palace's raiders reached the upper ferry at Thượng Độ before the Pivot's envoys stopped them. In 1046 the Pivot ended the Thunder Vein War: Thính Vũ kept the vein, and the south remembers. A century later the Tower struck at Phượng Minh's own vein, Đan Sơn Mạch, and lost.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a bare black rock ridge high in grey mountains, its surface split by glowing violet seams of light like veins. The signature is the branching violet seams themselves, glowing through the black rock like veins under skin. Storm cloud above. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the rock. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Lôi Trạch Thành
places.look: On a marshy river mouth by the sea, among old forest, stand the broken walls of a city whose stones are fused black and glassy, as if fired in a kiln. Over the old gate rises the shattered stump of a great drum tower, split down its middle. Reeds grow through the streets.
places.lore: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170 at the river mouth below its mountains. At the end of the Age of Seven Seats the lightning of Hầu Xuân Lôi's own tribulation burned it, and the next year its people moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Its dead lie on the bamboo hills inland, where Thu Phần Các now keeps the graves, and in autumn ghosts are said to sing old poems there.
places.history: Khải Lôi Môn built Lôi Trạch Thành in 170, ten years after Lý Thiên Cổ founded the Gate, at the river mouth below its mountains. It was the Gate's market and harbour, and its great drum tower answered the thunder of the peaks. The city buried its dead on the bamboo hills inland, away from the marsh. Three centuries after its founding Hầu Xuân Lôi, head of the Gate, was struck down by his own tribulation, and its lightning burned Lôi Trạch Thành. In 481 the survivors moved up the valley to Không Mông Thành. Thính Vũ Lâu took the land but never rebuilt the city, and the marsh crept into its streets. Nearly five centuries later Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the city's graves and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu, and since then the farmers of Ương Ca have heard singing from the graves each autumn.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on a reedy river-mouth marsh at the sea edge, among dark old trees: fragments of city wall with stones fused black and glassy, and the signature and tallest element, the split, shattered stump of a great round drum tower over a broken gate. Reeds and water in the old streets, no roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left glinting on the glassy stone. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Thu Phần Các
places.look: On a quiet bamboo hill inland from the ruins of Lôi Trạch, a pavilion of dark weathered wood with two small towers rises above slopes covered in old grave mounds. Between the bamboo, countless thin wooden slips, each brushed with a line of an old poem, hang on strings across the graves and clack softly in the wind.
places.lore: Thu Phần Các is a minor ma đạo sect of soul arts and grave wards, sworn to Thính Vũ Lâu by its founder and head Lý Hận Bích. It keeps the graves of Lôi Trạch Thành, where ghosts sing old poems in autumn. Its disciples copy down the poems the ghosts sing onto the wooden slips and hang them back over the graves. The villagers of Ương Ca stay away.
places.history: The bamboo hill was Lôi Trạch Thành's burial ground from the city's founding in the Age of First Gates, and its graves filled again when the tribulation lightning burned the city. After the survivors left for Không Mông Thành, the graves went untended for centuries and the bamboo grew over them. Mountain folk said that in autumn the dead sang old poems on the hill, and few went near. In 960 Lý Hận Bích founded Thu Phần Các among the graves, a sect of soul arts and grave wards, and swore it to Thính Vũ Lâu. By 962 the villagers of Ương Ca were hearing singing from the graves every autumn, and sang louder at planting to drown it. The pavilion keeps the hill silent in every other season, and its strings of poem slips grow longer with each autumn.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat miniature, vertical on a low bamboo-covered hill: a dark weathered wooden pavilion with two small stacked-roof towers in dark grey tile, the tallest outline on the hill, above slopes dotted with rounded grass grave mounds. The signature is many strings of thin pale wooden slips hung between the bamboo stems across the graves. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows of bamboo. No lit lanterns, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A walled grave court with a ward-stone at each corner, and a second tower for the soul arts.
Terraced halls climb the whole hill, and the slip strings reach down to its foot.

places.name: Phục Hổ Cương
places.look: A long, low ridge on the Kinh Trập highland, shaped like a great cat crouched with its head on its paws. Its exposed rock is banded in yellow and dark grey stripes, and the grass on it is flattened into long paths.
places.lore: A tiger-kind beast holds this ridge, where the storms wake the hills. Herders say the ridge itself was a tiger that lay down to wait for the first spring thunder and never rose. When thunder rolls over the highland, the beasts on the ridge roar back, and the villages below bar their doors.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a long low highland ridge shaped like a crouching cat, its bare rock banded in yellow and dark grey stripes, the signature; grass flattened in paths across it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Phần Vũ Đường
places.look: On the grassland inland from the red cliffs, a field of smoking volcanic vents opens in the ground, and around the largest a hall of red-brown stone climbs in tiers. The vent pits nearest the hall have stone sitting ledges cut into their lips, worn smooth by bodies. Above them a tall mast of black stone flies the crimson war banner Xích Hà Kỳ.
places.lore: Phần Vũ Đường is a minor sect of body tempering (luyện thể) under Phượng Minh Cung, whose disciples sit in the vents until their feathers burn and walk out reborn. Its head, Hùng Phần Vũ, born in Ngũ Thải Thành, founded it young in the vents where Xích Thành once stood. Phượng Minh lent it the Xích Hà Kỳ, the banner of the sect it destroyed, and everyone in the south reads the loan as both a trust and a warning. The mulberry town of Tang Điền belongs to it.
places.history: The vents of Đan Huyệt Châu fed Xích Thành Môn's fire arts from its founding in 250, and its banner Xích Hà Kỳ was woven from fire-silk spun in them. When Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn under writ in 590, the vent field was left without cultivators for more than four centuries. In 980 Hùng Phần Vũ was born in Ngũ Thải Thành, and a red feather fell on his cradle. In 1020 the young Hùng Phần Vũ founded Phần Vũ Đường in the vents where Xích Thành once stood, and Phượng Minh lent it the Xích Hà Kỳ. By 1025 its disciples were sitting in the vents until their feathers burned and walking out reborn; the first of them died trying. Since then the hall has sent its tempered fighters to the Palace's wars, and its sitting ledges are worn smooth.
places.art_brief: A minor sect seat miniature on flat grassland: a field of small smoking vent pits in reddish earth, and in its middle a tiered hall of red-brown stone with dark tile roofs climbing three short terraces. The signature and tallest element is a slender black stone mast flying a long crimson banner over the largest vent, whose lip is cut into stone ledges. Heat shimmer and thin smoke. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second tier of halls and a walled court around the sitting vents, with a stone bath for the burned.
A stepped red-stone hall rises high over the whole vent field, and the black mast stands on its top terrace.

places.name: Ngũ Thải Thành
places.look: A walled port city at a river mouth on the warm southern coast, its wards roofed in glazed tile of five colours, red, yellow, green, white and black, so that from the hills it looks like a bird's spread wing. A gate tower painted with a five-coloured bird faces the harbour.
places.lore: Xích Thành Môn built the city in 300 and named it for the five-coloured bird of Mount Đan Huyệt, the phoenix; Phượng Minh Cung has held it since 590. Each ward's guild keeps one colour of glaze, and quarrels between wards are settled by who repairs the most roofs. Hùng Phần Vũ, head of Phần Vũ Đường, was born here in 980, and a red feather fell on his cradle.
places.history: Xích Thành Môn built Ngũ Thải Thành in 300 on the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu as its port and market. Its potters glazed the roofs in five colours for the five-coloured bird of the old book, one colour to each ward. After Tôn Hà Khởi died, the city watched its own sect turn under Chu Liệt Nhật to burning villages. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn, and the city passed to the Palace with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu. Through the pirate years it barred its harbour by night, and its ships sailed with Phượng Minh's fleet in the Pirate Purge. In 980 Hùng Phần Vũ was born here, and a red feather fell on his cradle. Since he grew up and founded Phần Vũ Đường in the old vents, the city's young walk inland to try themselves.
places.art_brief: A walled port city miniature at a river mouth on a flat warm coast: rectangular walls, and the signature, ward after ward of glazed roofs in bands of red, yellow, green, white and black, fanning out like a wing; a tall gate tower facing the harbour as the tallest element, with a painted bird on its face. Boats at the quay. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the glazes shine. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A sixth ward of plain grey roofs for newcomers and a stone breakwater for the harbour.
A second wall ring up the river, and a five-roofed hall of the potters' guilds at the city's heart.

places.name: Thạch Cơ Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city on a flat stretch of coast, built around a long stone jetty that juts far out into the gulf. Most of the jetty is grey, sea-worn stone, but its outer end has been rebuilt in bright red stone that stands out against the water.
places.lore: Thạch Cơ Thành rose in 776 around the stone jetty where Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets gathered for the Pirate Purge under the Pivot's writ. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with red stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Old sailors grumble that the red end is unlucky; young ones say it is the strongest part.
places.history: Before the Purge this was a quiet stretch of shore within sight of the pirates' gulf. In 776 Đỗ Tinh Hà called the Pirate Purge, Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, and Thạch Cơ Thành rose around the stone jetty where they gathered. Five years later the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn with Ô Kình Hải dead, and the fleets came home here. The captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold were landed at the jetty and walked home to villages like Lô Châu. After the war the city stayed on as a port and a station for the Palace's ships in the gulf. In 1190 a storm cracked the jetty, and Phượng Minh rebuilt it with stone from the ruins of Xích Thành. Its red end is now the first thing incoming ships see.
places.art_brief: A walled harbour city miniature on a flat grassy coast: rectangular walls with grey-tile roofs and a modest harbour hall as the tallest building, and the signature, a long straight stone jetty running far out into blue water, grey along most of its length and bright red stone at its outer end. A few ships moored along it. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second jetty beside the first and a walled shipyard on the shore.
A fortified harbour city with a stone lighthouse at the red end of the jetty and a sea wall around the anchorage.

places.name: Tang Điền Trấn
places.look: A walled coastal town on rust-red earth, surrounded by long rows of mulberry bushes. Among the rows stand low two-storey silkworm sheds with slatted wooden walls, and in season the whole town smells of boiling cocoons.
places.lore: Mulberry fields have been planted in the red soil of Tang Điền since 200, and they feed the silkworms of the south. The town now belongs to Phần Vũ Đường. Its silk women say the red soil puts fire in the thread, and some claim that Xích Thành's fire-silk began with their worms.
places.history: Mulberry was first planted in the red soil of Tang Điền in 200, in the Age of First Gates, and its silkworms soon fed the looms of the south. When Xích Thành Môn rose among the red cliffs a generation later, the town fell under its shadow, and its silk women still claim the sect's fire-silk banner began with their worms. Under the heir who burned villages, the town's elders say, it paid in silk to be spared. After Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, Tang Điền passed with the rest of Đan Huyệt Châu to the Palace. The silk caravans that rest at Tang Âm carried its thread along the coast road. When Phần Vũ Đường was founded in the old vents, the town was given to the new hall, and its mulberry rows now feed the hall as well as the looms. The red earth and the slatted sheds are much as they were in the first planting.
places.art_brief: A low walled town miniature on a flat coast of rust-red soil: grey-tile roofs inside rectangular walls, surrounded by neat rows of green mulberry bushes, and the signature, long low two-storey sheds with slatted wooden walls among the rows. A small landing at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the red earth. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A reeling house by the shore and more silkworm sheds in the outer fields.
A brick-walled silk town with a dye works and a stone pier for the silk boats.

places.name: Cúc Viên Thôn
places.look: A small harbour village on a flat coast, its grey roofs half hidden by banked beds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums that fill every slope and yard. In autumn the gardens grow so thick that the paths between them cannot be seen.
places.lore: In the War of the Vermilion Caves in 586, the villagers of Cúc Viên hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums. The Palace has not forgotten, and its people still buy the village's flowers for the autumn rites. Every household keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person, just in case.
places.history: The chrysanthemum gardens of Cúc Viên were already old when Xích Thành Môn held the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. When the gate's heir turned to burning villages, Cúc Viên lived in fear of the red banners like every village on the coast. In the War of the Vermilion Caves, in 586, the villagers hid Phượng Minh's scouts among the chrysanthemums while the gate's patrols searched the shore. The scouts' reports are said to have helped the Palace bring the war to its end a few years later. When the coast passed to Phượng Minh, the Palace remembered the village and began to buy its flowers for the autumn rites. Through the pirate years the gardens were trampled more than once, but the beds always grew back. Every household still keeps one bed planted thick enough to hide a grown person.
places.art_brief: A tiny coastal village miniature: a few grey-tile roofs almost buried in the signature, banked mounds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums filling every yard and slope; a few small boats at a shore landing. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
