levels: A flower market under a roof by the landing and terraced beds up the dunes.
A walled hamlet with a small shrine to the hidden scouts amid the gardens.

places.name: Tang Âm Thôn
places.look: A harbour village on the coast road whose heart is a single vast old mulberry tree, its crown spread wide over a dusty caravan yard. Carts and pack animals stand in its shade, and the village houses face inward toward it.
places.lore: Since 600 the mulberry shade at Tang Âm has been the resting place of the silk caravans. Carters say the tree's shade is cooler than any roof, and that tying an animal to the trunk brings bad luck. The village lives on caravan inns and fodder.
places.history: The great mulberry at Tang Âm is older than the village, and herders sheltered under it long before any road ran along the coast. In 600, in the Age of the North Star Compact, the silk caravans of the south began to rest in its shade, and the village grew up around the yard to serve them. Its inns took in carters hauling thread from the red-soil fields of Tang Điền and goods bound for the port cities. In the pirate years the caravans ran fewer and under guard, and the villagers built their houses facing inward toward the tree. After the Pirate Purge the road filled again. The rule against tying an animal to the trunk is said to come from a carter whose mule tore down a limb, and whose luck went with it. Carters still touch the bark for luck before they leave.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a flat coast: a ring of grey-tile roofs facing inward around a bare earth yard, over which spreads the signature, one enormous wide-crowned mulberry tree; small carts parked in its shade. A small shore landing at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, dappled shade. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A long caravan inn with stables along the yard.
A walled caravan stop with a roofed gate on the coast road, the tree still at its centre.

places.name: Hồ Tâm Thôn
places.look: Behind the coastal dunes lies a round lake cut off from the sea, and the village sits on a small island in its middle, joined to the shore by a stone causeway. In the shallows beside the island stands a tall stone pillar notched with water marks, by which the villagers read the lake's strange tide. Their sea boats are dragged over the dunes to the beach.
places.lore: The lake at Hồ Tâm rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and since 900 Phượng Minh's scholars have not been able to say why. The villagers do not mind; they set their fish traps by the pillar. Children are told the lake breathes with the sea through the gills of a sleeping creature.
places.history: The lake behind the dunes has fed fishers since before the sects came to the coast, and the island village is older than anyone can remember. Under Xích Thành Môn, and then under Phượng Minh Cung, it paid its dues in dried fish. In 900 Phượng Minh's scholars came to study the lake that rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea, and they could not say why. They raised the notched stone pillar in the shallows to measure it, and their successors still come to read it. The villagers soon learned to set their fish traps by its marks. No explanation has ever been agreed on. The children's tale of a sleeping creature breathing with the sea is told more often than any scholar's.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature: a round calm lake behind pale sand dunes, a small island in its centre with a few grey-tile roofs, a narrow stone causeway to the shore. The signature is a tall notched stone pillar standing in the shallows beside the island. A few boats drawn up on the dunes. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A wider causeway and a boat slipway over the dunes.
A walled island hamlet with a scholars' tide hall built around the pillar.

places.name: Lô Châu Thôn
places.look: A river village on a low island of reed marsh, its houses raised on stilts with walls of bundled reeds lashed tight under grey-tile roofs. Paths of reed mats float between them, and the marsh around is cut into neat bays where reed is harvested.
places.lore: In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders carried off the whole village of Lô Châu; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. In 782, after the Purge, captives freed from Thôn Hải's hold came home and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family still keeps a reed bundle from that rebuilding hanging above the door, and the reed cutters are given the first seat at every feast.
places.history: Reed cutters lived on the marsh island of Lô Châu from the early ages, selling reed for thatch and mats up and down the river. In 765 Thôn Hải's raiders came up the river and carried off the whole village; only the reed cutters hidden in the marsh escaped. For years those few kept the island alive alone, cutting reed with no one to sell it to. When the Pirate Purge broke the pirates' hold, the captives held there were freed. In 782 they came home to Lô Châu and rebuilt it reed by reed. Every family hung a bundle from that rebuilding over its door, and the reed cutters were given the first seat at every feast. The custom has held ever since.
places.art_brief: A tiny village miniature on a low river island in a reed marsh: a few small stilted houses with pale bundled-reed walls under grey-tile roofs, the signature, linked by floating reed-mat paths; neat cut bays in the surrounding golden reeds. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A reed-weavers' shed and a timber jetty on the river.
A walled island hamlet on raised earth, its stilted houses joined by roofed boardwalks.

places.name: Đan Thạch Khoáng
places.look: A quarry cut into a red mountain, its face stepped in tall terraces of raw vermilion rock. Rough-cut red blocks lie in rows on the quarry floor, waiting to be dragged down the road.
places.lore: Red stone from Đan Thạch was cut for Xích Thành's walls from 280. Phượng Minh still quarries it for its own builders. Quarrymen say the stone holds the day's heat long after sunset, and sleep against the blocks in winter.
places.history: The red mountain of Đan Thạch was known for its colour long before anyone cut it. In 280 Xích Thành Môn began to quarry it for its walls, and the halls of the red cliff-gate rose out of its blocks. Through the gate's long rule the quarry fed its builders, and the terraces of the face grew deeper with each generation. Under the heir who burned villages the quarrymen worked for war. When Phượng Minh destroyed the gate under writ, the quarry passed to the Palace with the rest of the coast. Phượng Minh's builders have cut it ever since, and its red stone stands in walls across Đan Huyệt Châu. Quarrymen still sleep against the warm blocks in winter.
places.art_brief: A small quarry miniature on a red mountainside: the signature, a stepped quarry face of raw vermilion rock in tall terraces, with rows of rough red blocks on the floor and a dirt road leading away. Warm golden-hour light from the top left deepening the reds. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Dục Nhật Đảo
places.look: A forested island in the far south-eastern sea, its eastern shore facing open ocean where the sun rises straight out of the water. On that shore stands a great ring of sea-worn rock, an arch open to the sunrise, by which the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh opens. A single thatched hut sits under the trees above it.
places.lore: The first fishers of the gulf believed the sun bathed here every night before it rose. On this island Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, the Realm of the Sunrise Mulberry, at its first recorded opening, and the Thiên Nguyên calendar (Thiên Nguyên lịch) counts its years from that day. Since 700 he has lived here by the gate, the oldest living person, and has never left. Pilgrims come by boat to ask him about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year.
places.history: In the year 0 of the Thiên Nguyên calendar, Mạc Quy Khư entered the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh on Dục Nhật Đảo at its first recorded opening, and the calendar counts its years from that day. In 5 the first fishers of the gulf saw the sun rise out of the sea here, and believed it bathed at the island every night. Through the Wild Age and the ages of the sects, cultivators sailed here when the realm opened and went home again, and no sect ever held the island. Mạc Quy Khư's name grew with every age, until he was the oldest living cultivator in the world. In 700 he came to live on Dục Nhật Đảo by the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, and he has never left it since. By 1100 pilgrims were coming by boat to ask the hermit about the world before the sects, and he answers one question a year. The island is still unclaimed, and the fishers of the gulf still bow to its sunrise.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a small forested island in deep blue sea, its eastern shore of dark rock facing the rising sun. The signature is a great ring-shaped arch of sea-worn rock on that shore, open to the horizon, with a faint warm glow within it. Under the trees above, one tiny thatched hut no larger than a speck. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, a gold path on the water. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Đồ Nam Đảo
places.look: A low grassy island in the southern sea, its crown pressed into a vast shallow hollow, as if something enormous had lain there. The grass in the hollow grows in long swirled streaks like the print of feathers, and seabirds wheel over it in their thousands.
places.lore: The great Bằng is said to rest on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, as the old book tells of the bird that rises beyond the clouds and sets out southward. Fishers say the hollow is its bed, and that the wind there always blows toward the south. No one lives on the island; sailors land only to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind.
places.history: Fishers of the southern gulf knew the island from the earliest ages, a bare grassy hump with no spring and no harbour. By 350, in the Age of Seven Seats, the tale was told that the great Bằng rested on Đồ Nam Đảo before its flight to the south, and the hollow on its crown was called its bed. Sailors began to leave fish in the hollow for a fair wind southward, a custom that has never stopped. In the pirate years of the Age of the North Star Compact, Thôn Hải's ships are said to have anchored off the island but never landed, holding it unlucky. After the Purge the fishers came back to its waters. No sect has ever claimed it, and no one has ever dug the hollow.
places.art_brief: A natural-site miniature with no roofline: a low green island in blue sea, its crown pressed into a broad shallow oval hollow, the signature, with grass inside it combed in long swirling feather-like streaks. Small white seabirds circling as specks. Warm golden-hour light from the top left raking across the grass. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Xích Thành Môn
places.look: On the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, cliffs of deep red rock rise in rounded tiers like banks of rosy cloud above the sea. Into them are cut the broken terraces and gutted halls of the old gate, their fire-blackened walls open to the sky, with fresh pale quarry scars where stone has lately been taken away.
places.lore: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn here in 250, among red cliffs and vents where the rock rises like a rosy cloud. Its banner Xích Hà Kỳ was woven from fire-silk spun in the vents. Under his heir Chu Liệt Nhật the sect burned villages to feed its fire arts, and Phượng Minh destroyed it under the Compact's first writ. Herders do not graze here; they say the cliffs are still warm at night.
places.history: Tôn Hà Khởi founded Xích Thành Môn in 250 among the red cliffs and vents of Đan Huyệt Châu, and in 260 the sect wove its war banner, the Xích Hà Kỳ, from fire-silk spun in the vents. Within a generation its walls were cut from the red stone of Đan Thạch, and soon after it built Ngũ Thải Thành on the coast. Tôn Hà Khởi died in 560, and his heir Chu Liệt Nhật turned the sect to burning villages to feed its fire arts. After eleven villages had burned, Phượng Minh Cung asked the Pivot for a writ, and the first writ of the North Star Compact was granted. In 590 Phượng Minh destroyed Xích Thành Môn with Chu Liệt Nhật, and the Xích Hà Kỳ went to hang in the Palace's hall. Four centuries later the banner was lent to Phần Vũ Đường, which revived the fire arts in the vents inland. In the last years of the Age of Vein Wars, Phượng Minh took stone from these ruins to rebuild the cracked jetty of Thạch Cơ Thành.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals on a steppe coast above the sea: deep red cliffs in rounded stacked tiers like rosy cloud banks, the signature, with broken terraces and roofless, fire-blackened stone halls cut into them; a few pale fresh quarry scars on the red rock. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left turning the cliffs crimson. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Thôn Hải Môn
places.look: A small forested islet in the southern gulf, ringed by rocks. At the waterline gapes the black mouth of a sea cave large enough to take a ship, its rim scorched and the stumps of a broken log boom still standing across it. Charred timbers of the old hold lie heaped inside the entrance.
places.lore: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on this islet in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn, the Gate That Swallows the Sea, and for over a century its ships raided the southern coasts. The Purge ended here in 781 when he died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. Treasure seekers still row out to dig in the ash, and some do not row back.
places.history: Ô Kình Hải gathered pirates on an islet of the southern gulf in 640 and founded Thôn Hải Môn; fishers say the pirate ships lay hidden in the great sea cave. A century and more later his pirates burned the pearl harbour of Châu Lệ Cảng, and soon after they carried off the whole village of Lô Châu. Then Đỗ Tinh Hà of Thiên Xu Tông called the Pirate Purge, and Phượng Minh's and Lạc Hà's fleets sailed under the Pivot's writ, while the watchers on the cliffs of Vọng Hải could see the pirates' sails a day before they landed. In 781 the Purge ended at Thôn Hải Môn: Ô Kình Hải died on his islet, and his sabre Kình Nha was lost in the burning hold. The captives held there were freed and went home to rebuild their villages. The islet has lain in Phượng Minh's land ever since, and no one has settled it.
places.art_brief: A ruin miniature of broken verticals: a small rocky islet with dark green trees in blue gulf water, and the signature, a huge black sea-cave mouth at the waterline with a scorched rim and the broken stumps of a log boom standing in the water across it; heaped charred timbers just inside. No roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, deep shadow in the cave. No text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Vạn Xà Lâm
places.look: Deep jungle at the far end of Đan Huyệt Châu, where giant strangler figs have wrapped and swallowed older trees. Their grey roots coil over a black, still pool like nests of snakes, and real snakes lie sunning on them.
places.lore: The farthest beast lair from any town, the forest is home to snakes of every kind and the beasts that eat them. Alchemists' collectors come for venom and shed skins in the dry season, never in the wet. Locals say one snake in the forest is old enough to remember Xích Thành, and does not like fire.

places.name: Chu Sa Tuyền
places.look: In a jungle clearing, a single round hot spring boils up blood-red from the ground, steaming hard, and its overflow runs away through the trees in a bright vermilion stream. The jungle around is pale with rising steam.
places.lore: A red hot spring in the phoenix's cinnabar land, held by Phượng Minh Cung. Its water tastes of iron and stains skin pink for days. Fire cultivators come to soak after training in the vents, and herbalists scrape the red crust from the stream bed.

places.name: Chúc Dung Khẩu
places.look: On the east coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, a low volcanic cone of black rock opens in a wide crater whose lip is shaped like an open mouth. Inside, lava glows orange, and a thin tongue of it creeps down a notch in the rim, hissing where it meets wet rock.
places.lore: Named for the fire god Chúc Dung, the vent is the most dangerous place in the land of the vermilion caves, and Phượng Minh Cung keeps watch on it. Fire cultivators say its heat teaches what no vent inland can, if they live through the lesson. Fishers along the coast read its smoke for weather.
